   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From:Iain D. Smith, PITLOCHRY

Dear Sirs,

Could you please advise me on
how to clear the key buffer
before an input as, at times,old
key presses get carried on to
the next input.

e.g.,  GET a
       CLS
       INPUT "Name" PL1$


The above program will often put
into PL1$ "3", if you press 3
for GET a. You then have to use
DELETE before inputting pl1$. I
have tried using different POKE
SVAR's but to no avail.

The program to lock out sectors
might have been handy on my
corrupted disc if I had made a
back up copy before it happened.

Is there a POKE to disable the
Y/N? on a FORMAT?
                      IAIN

POKE 23611,PEEK 23611 BAND 223
just before the INPUT cures the
input bug. It works 99 times out
of a hundred.In a situation that
it doesn't, try DPOKE 23701,257
FIRST as well as the other POKE.
I know of only one occasion that
the first POKE alone didn't work
fully and that was in HI-BAR I
think. Sorry, I don't know of a
POKE to disable the FORMAT Y/N;
does anyone else?
                        - Brian

From: Alan D. Cox, DYFED


Dear Ron and Brian,

I refer to my earlier letter on
the 'reverse listing' bug and
the supporting comment from
Stuart M. Burton of Poole in
this month's OUTLET.

Following an open invitation in
a recent FORMAT I wrote to Andy
Wright at BETASOFT about this
bug and he offered an explan-
ation based on the postulated
use of indented listings.

However I do not normally use
such listings, so this did not
solve my particular problem.

I have found a way to create the
effect consistently, albeit so
far only with one particular
program and have sent Andy a
disk demonstrating this. I await
his response.

I pointed out to Andy that Mr
Burton had the same problem and
suggested that once he had found
the cause either he or I should
write further to OUTLET.

I cannot guarantee it works for
all programs but try listing
high,e.g., LIST 8000, reject the
scroll, then list low,e.g., LIST
7000, reject the scroll and then
up arrow. In my case this gives
the colour bars superimposed on
the listing, and touching the
keyboard gives a full reset.

On a second topic, I recently
joined the local Computer User
Group, and because I was the
only member with a SAM Coupe the
Editor of the Newsletter asked
me to write a piece about it. He
wanted the article quickly, so
there was no time to explore
transferring the piece from
computer to computer so he had
to re-type it into his machine
(remind me not to volunteer to
edit the Newsletter!) - he uses
a PC with TOP COPY PLUS. How-
ever, this was clearly crazy as
a long-term solution so we have
been experimenting with other
methods.

The first arises because the
Editor still has a Spectrum+
set-up with microdrives.

He can transfer from Spectrum to
PC using the Interface 1 serial
port and the MOVE command, as
follows:

  10 CLOSE #4
  20 FORMAT "b";1200
  30 OPEN #4;"b"
  40 INPUT "ENTER FILE NAME";N$
  50 MOVE "M";2;N$ TO #4
  60 CLOSE #4
  70 STOP

At the PC end he uses the 'Mite'
software package about which I
know nothing except that it
works. Now 'WORDMASTER' saves
documents as CODE files, so the
only gap in the chain is that of
a Spectrum reading a SAM CODE
file - SAM can of course read a
Spectrum/Disciple CODE file.

However, I suppose not surpris-
ingly the converse is not true:
it would have been clever for
the writer of the Disciple
software to anticipate the SAM
protocols!

It is not a great problem - I
imagine that you do something
like it every day - but for the
record - the way to do it is to
use the READ AT command on the
Disciple to read what is needed
into the Spectrum memory and
then SAVE it as a real Spectrum
CODE file.

SAM CODE files have, on their
first sector, a nine-byte
header, followed by 501 bytes of
the file, ending with a two-byte


pointer to the next track/sector
used. Subsequent track/sectors
have no header but do have the
pointer to the next track/
sector. Surprisingly, there does
not appear to be an end-of-file
marker in the last sector.

Thus to make the transfer, take
a clean(i.e.,reformatted or else
with all files deleted) disk and
save the SAM CODE file on it.
This is to make things easy,
since you then know that the
file starts on track 4, sector 1
and continues in order. Working
out the more general case would
not be difficult, but seems to
me unnecessary in the circumst-
ances. Also note the length of
the file.

Then transfer to the Spectrum,
put the disk into the Disciple
drive, type in the following
program, then run it. You will
end up with a Spectrum CODE file
with the same name as the SAM
one with "s" added at the begin-
ning and if necessary truncated
to 10 characters in all.
 10 REM Conversion program
 20 INPUT "name of file ?";n$
 25 LET n$=n$( TO 9)
 30 INPUT "Length of file ?";L
 40 LET z=INT(L/512)+1
 50 FOR n=1 to z
 60 LOAD @1,4+INT (n/10),n-10
    *INT(n/10),40000-9+510*(n-1)
 70 NEXT n
 80 LET z$="s"+n$
 90 SAVE d1;z$CODE 40000,L
 100 STOP

However, this is still not ideal
from my point of view, if for no
other reason than that I used to
find microdrives irritating and
unreliable. The obvious medium
is to use 3.5 inch floppy disks
at both ends. The major apparent
snag to this is that whereas SAM
formats a disk with 80 tracks
per side and 10 sectors per
track, the PC, using DD/DS
disks, uses 80 tracks per side
but only 9 sectors per track.

However,to my surprise, although
the sectors must be of different
physical size, SAM can read
sectors 1 to 9 on a PC track
using READ AT, although he does
not like trying to find the
tenth sector! I assume that the


sector 'marks' on the disk must
be electronic, not physical.

There are minor points to sort
out, since the PC starts with 2
boot sectors, which have no
apparent SAM equivalent, and
then has 6 sectors of a File
Allocation Table (or FAT), which
I think corresponds to the
memory map in the SAM directory
entry for a file, and then 6
sectors of something called
Directory, which I imagine is
like the first part of a SAM
Directory.

I have to confess that I have
yet to understand fully where
the PC puts its files, since I
have only had a single example
to experiment with.

If any reader can help, then I
would be grateful for the
information.

Of course, the final stage of
the experiment is to see whether
the PC can duplicate the SAM
READ AT command. If so then all
that remains at the SAM end is
to arrange for files to be
written on only sectors 1 to 9
of each track, which should not
be difficult using WRITE AT.
This end of the experiment is
not under my control, and would
be,I judge,of lesser interest to
OUTLET readers, so I think it
worth informing you of the above
before the experiment is
completed.
         All best wishes
           Alan D.Cox

Brian Cavers to Alan Cox

I couldn't get your listing bug
to show itself using the method
you describe. It probably just
depends on the program - perhaps
there is something odd about the
programs in which it resets,e.g.
code in REMS or Line 0's?

Regarding transferring SAM code
files to Spectrum, have you
forgotten SAMTOD in Issue 46?
Perhaps you didn't have that
issue. In any event it works in
a similar way to your method but
the file doesn't need to be the
first on a clean disc. SAMTOD
finds the first sector from the
directory. The "flag" for the
final sector are two zeros at
the end.

I had the same problem with a PC
disc that someone sent in with a
HUGE instruction manual for a
program contributed to OUTLET. I
had that disc months and in the
end I think I crudely loaded in
all the sectors and tried to
piece together the text but I
got in such a mess I gave up! I
never did have any info on the
directory system.

I've an idea that an early SAM
SUPPLEMENT disc had a PC file
loader - might be worth studying
the BASIC?

                        - Brian

Mr. L.A.G.Ross, - Renfrewshire.

Dear Brian & Ron,

I am delighted with Outwrite.
Perhaps as time goes on, it
could be provided with a better
'insert' mode - like the
auto-insert of Tasword 3 or the
Extended mode of Wordmaster.

One of my Sam disc drives lodges
badly causing "check disc drive"
error messages. Several phone
enquiries have produced advice
on excessively tight screwing
in; the need to press in the
blue release tag;the possibility
of slight corrosion in the
factory etc. I believe you have
had correspondence about this.
Any solutions?

The Sam, to my surprise, works
quite well. No trouble with tape
loading. Specmaker is first rate
and easy to use, Speclone less
so. All my word processors
(except Tasword 3), data banks
and 48K graphic programmes are
safely transferred. But it took
Sam Computers Ltd. five weeks to
send a made up lead (Sam to
Philips B/W m monitor).

Many thanks once again for a
wonderful magazine.

        Yours sincerely,

           L.A.G.Ross

Brian Cavers to I.A.G. Ross

It's unlikely that OUTWRITE will
have an "auto-insert" (I presume
that means"pushing existing text
ahead of the cursor as you type
in new text?). You see, OUTWRITE
is a budget-priced wordprocessor
similar to Tasword 2 was on the
Spectrum. Notice Tasman never
upgraded Tasword 2? No, they
brought out completely new word
processors: Tasword 3 etc. It's
often easier to start again than
try to re-write some parts of
existing code. Only a programmer
can decide what is practical.
Anyway, to insert text, simply
press SYMBOL + CURSOR DOWN to
make space, type - then reform
the paragraph afterwards.

We have been plagued with disc
errors ourselves! I can only
suggest you try the following...

Switch the drives over, i.e.,
drive 1 in 2 position, drive 2
in drive 1 position.

Try a different step rate, e.g.,
POKE DVAR 3,3 for drive 1, POKE
DVAR 4,3, for drive 2.

Check you are not using an early
version of MASTERDOS with the
new, 2-meg drives. MASTERDOS 13
or thereabouts may not be able
to cope with the new drives.

If all else fails, return the
dodgy drive to PBT for repair!
                        - Brian

From Mike Haine, LEAMINGTON

Dear Ron and Brian,

Slightly delayed congratulations
on the 50th issue.

Glad to hear Bob Wilkinson's
OUTWRITE is being revised. I
must confess I only use it where
I need the extra text space.
Apart from that and the smoother
and faster key response, I much
prefer the Tasword 2 with my
modifications to the BASIC.

My main objections to OUTWRITE
are the awkward choice of
control keys and the INSERT
function which messes up a
normal paragraph structure in

the text if used on the first
line of the paragraph and if
there is no blank line at the
end of the paragraph. Why not
just look for a space in the
first char position of the line?

The omission of a proper INSERT
facility is a major limitation.
In TAS2 to insert at the cursor
one just presses CNTRL I and
then types the insert. Then
pressing F3,causes the whole
para to reformat without affect-
ing the part before the insert.
This is vastly better than
OUTWRITE in its present form.

On the subject of control key
choices; it is beyond my
understanding why one had to
press EDIT and then a key.

There are surely enough options
to make this unnecessary?

It is puzzling to know why the
disc functions aren't all dealt
with by going to a menu in
BASIC! One certainly doesn't
want to have a disc DIR every-
time one uses the disc.

The obvious thing is to have the
text handling key controls in
text mode, while for the disc
handling and printing a single
key press (For Tas2 this is F9)
gives a menu (in Basic) to allow
choice of disc number and/or
function.

The Print option can also better
be handled from BASIC.

In my mod. to Tas2, F9 gives a
popup menu for choice of disc,
(1,2, or higher for RAM discs).


Pressing the digit immediately
replaces the menu by one with
numbered items which allows
choice of short DIR, full DIR or
others. I use one DIR d "l*"
which lists all files starting
with "l" (These are my letter
files).

Other such options are possible.
Again the single key press
(1to9) gives the chosen DIR. If
the list is longer than the
screen length, then the scroll
query can be answered with any
key other than "n".

However, if the list on the
screen contains the item of
interest then "n" prevents the
scroll and gives the next menu
(by use of an "ON ERROR GOTO")
allows for the choice of the
disc function (LOAD. MERGE.
SAVE. ERASE). (It is useful to
have the list on screen when
typing in the name.)

Pressing "l","m"."s","E" then
gives query for name. Here, if
the item has been loaded, (such
as for extension etc.) so that
the name has already been
specified then just pressing
RETURN is all that is necessary.

A query to confirm is included
for safety. This may seem a bit

longwinded since some of the
functions(e.g.,the DIRs) may not
be required. However, the menu
items are skipped if any key
other than "0 to 9" or "l,m,s,E"
in the function menu. e.g. if
one presses "d" from the main
menu followed by any letter and
"l"(e.g.,"ll" you get the "NAME?
"query for loading from disc 1.

If you want to skip from that
point "RETURN" takes you back to
the main menu. To get back into
text mode just press "RETURN"
again.

The lines defining these
features can be be used directly
in OUTWRITE. (just with a change
of line number).

My main Tas 2 menu has an item
"PRINT".This gives the option to
print in 2, 64-character columns
(condensed mode). I have added
this item to OUTWRITE together
with a short Basic routine to
perform the 2-column print
function. Why on earth is the
delete key not used properly to
delete the character on which
the cursor sits?

This is presumably because the
cursor obscures the character.
Please do change this! I wonder
how long it will take you
computer wizards to realise that
required items in lists are much
easier to locate if the lists
are in alphabetical order, (see
my article in OUTLET 51).

The Help pages need reorganising
in this way. The main menu
obtained on loading is weak in
this way, each item should start
with a key word, e.g., the first
item should be "TEXT mode" and
the second "DRIVE change".

The user after the first few
times will need to grasp the
function with least delay and
certainly not to have to read a
whole line before finding the
word key to the function.I much
prefer pop up menus (and I find
most people who are using my
mods agree).I found a difficulty
at first with these in that one
tended to find that their
printing, such as by:-PRINT #0;
"LOAD. SAVE. etc would cause the
main text to scroll up.

This was because the control
space at the bottom of the
screen was over-filled.

This is easily overcome by the
use of
  CALL 337:PRINT #0;".....

The Call clears the control
space of the screen without
affecting the main part.

There are quite a few other
improvements which could be
suggested for OUTWRITE. One
example is to have the facility
to use the FONTS in the print-
ing. If RJW and yourselves would
be interested I should be happy
to co-operate in its
development.

Let me add that I am full of
admiration for the author of any
program of the magnitude of
OUTWRITE. The sheer magnitude of
the task of writing and de-
bugging so long a program would
be quite beyond me. This alone
surely makes it all the more
desirable for users to put in
suggestion and criticisms to
help the prog reach a further
stage of perfection.

           Mike Haine
.

Brian Cavers to Mike Haine

Thanks for all your ideas, Mike.
All feedback on OUTWRITE is
noted for the future upgrade. I
must just make some comments
in reply though...

The control keys are NOT awkward
as you say but it is merely that
they are not to your preference
and that anything new is unfam-
iliar and therefore may SEEM
awkward to YOU. You speak of
pressing EDIT then a key as if
this is a problem. Clearly there
are not enough extra keys to
provide a single keypress for
every function. The alternative
is a SHIFTED key which differs
only because you don't RELEASE
between keys. Right?

You'll find all the actual disc
access is in BASIC anyway so you
can easily remove the DIR if
required.I agree printing may be
better from BASIC or at least
started in BASIC so it could be
modified easily, for instance,
multiple copies, adding,removing
a linefeed, etc.

The DELETE key IS used properly.
Again, it is your concept of how
it should be that conflicts. Who
is the authority to say DELETE
must delete the character on
which the cursor is sitting? Is
it written somewhere in tablets
of stone? I'm happy with it. You
have simply got used to just ONE
method of doing it and assume it
to be THE method.

I'm sorry Mike but our software
is our bread and butter and I
must defend it in the same mood
that you attack it! If you had
simply said, "I don't agree with
the method used by DELETE, much
preferring another method" I
would have more sympathy but if
you say, "Why on earth is the
delete key not use properly" I
have to reply in like manner!

Again, you say that the help
pages would be better in alpha-
betical order - they ARE in
alphabetical order!!!! The only
possible exceptions are where
there are not enough letters of
the alphabet! Obviously "C"could
not be used to copy a block as
"C" is already used to CLEAR.

I'm baffled by what you mean...
"L - LOAD, M - MERGE, P - PRINT"
etc., etc. is straight off our
help pages and anyone can see is
in alphabetical order and is
simplicity itself.

You'll be pleased to hear that
the new upgrade is likely to
have pop-up menus which make it
easier for the beginner but will
not hamper the experienced user.

Thanks for your offer of help in
printing out fonts but we prefer
not to get involved in too much
extra work. However, if you can
come up with say, a stand-alone
USER BASIC merge routine I would
be glad to put it in OUTLET as
an "extra".

Anyway, all your ideas are noted
but remember, this is a commerc-
ial enterprise and we have to
set a limit on time and money
invested in further changes. It
is likely all the work now being
put in further improvements will
not receive a reasonable return
because the market is too small.
Why do you think Tasword keeps
out of it?

We've come to accept that what-
ever we do, someone will object
and say it should have been done
a different way! However, keep
sending in your comments and
ideas and we'll do the best we
can!
                        - Brian

From Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

Dear Ron and Brian

As a follow up to my previous
letter about firms and your
comments, without wishing to
start a serial, can I add the
following points to put things
into perspective and leave the
reader to decide if it was a
case of complaining about
nothing or that the firm should
reconsider its policies?

If I dealt with all the problems
over say, the last 8 years,
relating to computers and
associated firms I would fill
all the letters allocation in
this issue.  [mercy! - BC]

If I detailed all the problems
associated with dealing with
radio, electronics, electrical-
related firms - my main hobby,
interests and trade over the
last 40 years (that's giving age
away),I would be hard pressed to
fill half a screen.

I would not dispute the costs in
replying to queries, however,
time is irrelevant when the firm
is happy to spend time answering
'phone queries but is too busy
to answer a letter. From
experience a 'phone call goes
into 10 min to 20 min.A test run
on answering a letter takes 2-3
mins. to do a simple answer. The
crunch to remember also is a
letter costs you 2 stamps.

How much for a daytime call of
1/2 hour while the firm hunts
for answers or finds inform-
ation. Chezron does not have a
'phone number. why? I bet it's
because it is too time-wasting.

Let's compare two examples...

I needed some parts for a car
tape player, take-up gear,
pivot, spring, etc., all small
parts - estimated cost `8. I
found the address of the main
importer. Now such firms often
only deal with agents in order
values of many thousands of
pounds. Still I tried. My letter
was passed to their agent, they
sent me a photocopy of the
relevant page of the service


manual and exploded view so I
could identify the parts I
required. I ordered and had the
parts. It all took about 2
weeks. cost `12.

A firm has an ad in a mag. for
colour monitors. no price, type,
size or any info. Now what is a
colour monitor -`150 or more? So
I ask. No reply. I then buy two
colour monitors elsewhere (fair
comment, the firm did not know I
was likely to buy 2).

Incidentally, enquiries to firms
take up all of 3 or 4 lines so
cannot contain much waffle or
stray from the point. They do
get longer when the firm messes
me about.

Finally all the following relate
to one firm and a run up to
being told I was "selfish" to
expect replies.

There are very limited choice of
firms relating to some aspects
of computers. (No way related to
the following but as an example
if your SAM goes duff how many
firms can you choose from to get
it repaired? There's not much
point hunting through yellow
Pages. As I said this experience
has nothing to do with SAM.)


Before we start and so readers
can join in lets all practice
the chorus together......."NO
REPLY"

I had an item damaged in the
post.I needed a written estimate
to make a claim.

NO REPLY.


I guessed and made the claim
without. luckily, the PO paid up
on my own estimate.

I now needed it repaired, asked
if it could be done and an idea
of cost. I told them exactly the
2 parts to be replaced and that
the item was working otherwise
O.K.

NO REPLY.

I asked if they could supply the
parts (and I would do it myself,
having hunted through a number
of other catalogues without
results for suitable parts. This
firm was suposed to be the
(only?) repairer for this item).

NO REPLY.


I gave up on this and now have a
temporary "repair" and the item
working.


I was having a different problem
with another item. Guess who
repairs them? So, try again.

NO REPLY.

I asked about selling me some-
thing.Yes you have guessed it...

NO REPLY.(est. value over `100).

You'd think I'd have learnt my
lesson by now,no - not me, I'm a
glutton for punishment.

I needed another written esti-
mate for an insurance-type claim
and gave precise details of the
parts to be replaced, number and
even RS catalogue number. No, I
did not want a detailed quote,
simply an order of cast for 9
parts and estimated two hours
work to unsolder old, resolder
new, and set up, to at least
start the insurance claim off.
NO REPLY.

I sent off some money for some
goods, month later...

(all together now!) NO REPLY!!

Why, you might ask, send money
to a firm that has declined to
be of service in the past? I
simply could not, at the time,
find anyone else selling it. See
what I mean about limited choice
of firms?

I asked why non-delivery.

NO RE.. (this is getting boring)

After a couple of weeks I tried
phoning. At last, A REPLY - an
answering machine! I actually
phoned twice but still no goods.

I contacted my bank to confirm
the cheque was cashed: a week
after it was sent - two months
earlier.I've a photocopy to make
sure it was correctly cashed.

At this point I write to the
editor of mag where they advert-
ise out of frustration and ask
if the firm actually exists and
get the "selfish to expect
replies" comment and usual
excuses for firms not replying.
(sorry Brian, same lines as your
comments, do you both have the
same script writer?).

There was comment in the answer
from the editor about the firm
not knowing who I was!! Perhaps,
not only do they not reply but
don't read mail either.

I also wrote to the firm stating
that the order is cancelled and
ask for a refund. I received a
letter giving the reason for
non-replies as "too busy" and
etc. and instead of my request
to refund, I receive the item.

It was not all that I expected
so again I wrote and got a re-
placement with all of the items.

Now I would think it unlikely
all my letters or all replies
went astray or were overlooked.

I leave it to readers to draw
their own conclusions as to if
such a firm is offering good
service or not.

                 Malcolm Perry

Brian Cavers to Malcom Perry

Well,it looks like their service
is pretty pathetic. My comments
last month were based on general
mistakes that people make such
as asking for information and
advice not directly related to
the company's products or over-
reacting too soon. I can only
add a few comments...

Years ago I believed that good
service helped sales and used to
comfort myself that bad service
in say, a shop, meant they would
lose custom. I no longer believe
it is has much affect on sales.
If it did,all these places would
go out of business but clearly
they go on and on and on.

In contrast, we ourselves have
strived to give good service -
not because it's good for

From: Alan D. Cox, DYFED

Dear Ron and Brian,

I refer to my earlier letter on the 'reverse listing' bug and the supporting comment from Stuart M. Burton of Poole in this month's OUTLET.

Following an open invitation in a recent FORMAT I wrote to Andy Wright at BETASOFT about this bug and he offered an explan- ation based on the postulated use of indented listings.

However I do not normally use such listings, so this did not solve my particular problem.

I have found a way to create the effect consistently, albeit so far only with one particular program and have sent Andy a disk demonstrating this. I await his response.

I pointed out to Andy that Mr Burton had the same problem and suggested that once he had found the cause either he or I should write further to OUTLET.

I cannot guarantee it works for all programs but try listing high,e.g., LIST 8000, reject the scroll, then list low,e.g., LIST 7000, reject the scroll and then up arrow. In my case this gives the colour bars superimposed on the listing, and touching the keyboard gives a full reset.

On a second topic, I recently joined the local Computer User Group, and because I was the only member with a SAM Coupe the Editor of the Newsletter asked me to write a piece about it. He wanted the article quickly, so there was no time to explore transferring the piece from computer to computer so he had to re-type it into his machine (remind me not to volunteer to edit the Newsletter!) - he uses a PC with TOP COPY PLUS. How- ever, this was clearly crazy as a long-term solution so we have been experimenting with other methods.

The first arises because the Editor still has a Spectrum+ set-up with microdrives.

He can transfer from Spectrum to PC using the Interface 1 serial port and the MOVE command, as follows:

10 CLOSE #4 20 FORMAT "b";1200 30 OPEN #4;"b" 40 INPUT "ENTER FILE NAME";N$ 50 MOVE "M";2;N$ TO #4 60 CLOSE #4 70 STOP

At the PC end he uses the 'Mite' software package about which I know nothing except that it works. Now 'WORDMASTER' saves documents as CODE files, so the only gap in the chain is that of a Spectrum reading a SAM CODE file - SAM can of course read a Spectrum/Disciple CODE file.

However, I suppose not surpris- ingly the converse is not true: it would have been clever for the writer of the Disciple software to anticipate the SAM protocols!

It is not a great problem - I imagine that you do something like it every day - but for the record - the way to do it is to use the READ AT command on the Disciple to read what is needed into the Spectrum memory and then SAVE it as a real Spectrum CODE file.

SAM CODE files have, on their first sector, a nine-byte header, followed by 501 bytes of the file, ending with a two-byte

pointer to the next track/sector used. Subsequent track/sectors have no header but do have the pointer to the next track/ sector. Surprisingly, there does not appear to be an end-of-file marker in the last sector.

Thus to make the transfer, take a clean(i.e.,reformatted or else with all files deleted) disk and save the SAM CODE file on it. This is to make things easy, since you then know that the file starts on track 4, sector 1 and continues in order. Working out the more general case would not be difficult, but seems to me unnecessary in the circumst- ances. Also note the length of the file.

Then transfer to the Spectrum, put the disk into the Disciple drive, type in the following program, then run it. You will end up with a Spectrum CODE file with the same name as the SAM one with "s" added at the begin- ning and if necessary truncated to 10 characters in all. 10 REM Conversion program 20 INPUT "name of file ?";n$ 25 LET n$=n$( TO 9) 30 INPUT "Length of file ?";L 40 LET z=INT(L/512)+1 50 FOR n=1 to z 60 LOAD @1,4+INT (n/10),n-10

```text
    *INT(n/10),40000-9+510*(n-1)
```

70 NEXT n 80 LET z$="s"+n$ 90 SAVE d1;z$CODE 40000,L 100 STOP

However, this is still not ideal from my point of view, if for no other reason than that I used to find microdrives irritating and unreliable. The obvious medium is to use 3.5 inch floppy disks at both ends. The major apparent snag to this is that whereas SAM formats a disk with 80 tracks per side and 10 sectors per track, the PC, using DD/DS disks, uses 80 tracks per side but only 9 sectors per track.

However,to my surprise, although the sectors must be of different physical size, SAM can read sectors 1 to 9 on a PC track using READ AT, although he does not like trying to find the tenth sector! I assume that the

sector 'marks' on the disk must be electronic, not physical.

There are minor points to sort out, since the PC starts with 2 boot sectors, which have no apparent SAM equivalent, and then has 6 sectors of a File Allocation Table (or FAT), which I think corresponds to the memory map in the SAM directory entry for a file, and then 6 sectors of something called Directory, which I imagine is like the first part of a SAM Directory.

I have to confess that I have yet to understand fully where the PC puts its files, since I have only had a single example to experiment with.

If any reader can help, then I would be grateful for the information.

Of course, the final stage of the experiment is to see whether the PC can duplicate the SAM READ AT command. If so then all that remains at the SAM end is to arrange for files to be written on only sectors 1 to 9 of each track, which should not be difficult using WRITE AT. This end of the experiment is not under my control, and would be,I judge,of lesser interest to OUTLET readers, so I think it worth informing you of the above before the experiment is completed. All best wishes Alan D.Cox

From Mike Haine, LEAMINGTON

Dear Ron and Brian,

Slightly delayed congratulations on the 50th issue.

Glad to hear Bob Wilkinson's OUTWRITE is being revised. I must confess I only use it where I need the extra text space. Apart from that and the smoother and faster key response, I much prefer the Tasword 2 with my modifications to the BASIC.

My main objections to OUTWRITE are the awkward choice of control keys and the INSERT function which messes up a normal paragraph structure in

the text if used on the first line of the paragraph and if there is no blank line at the end of the paragraph. Why not just look for a space in the first char position of the line?

The omission of a proper INSERT facility is a major limitation. In TAS2 to insert at the cursor one just presses CNTRL I and then types the insert. Then pressing F3,causes the whole para to reformat without affect- ing the part before the insert. This is vastly better than OUTWRITE in its present form.

On the subject of control key choices; it is beyond my understanding why one had to press EDIT and then a key.

There are surely enough options to make this unnecessary?

It is puzzling to know why the disc functions aren't all dealt with by going to a menu in BASIC! One certainly doesn't want to have a disc DIR every- time one uses the disc.

The obvious thing is to have the text handling key controls in text mode, while for the disc handling and printing a single key press (For Tas2 this is F9) gives a menu (in Basic) to allow choice of disc number and/or function.

The Print option can also better be handled from BASIC.

In my mod. to Tas2, F9 gives a popup menu for choice of disc, (1,2, or higher for RAM discs).

Pressing the digit immediately replaces the menu by one with numbered items which allows choice of short DIR, full DIR or others. I use one DIR d "l*" which lists all files starting with "l" (These are my letter files).

Other such options are possible. Again the single key press (1to9) gives the chosen DIR. If the list is longer than the screen length, then the scroll query can be answered with any key other than "n".

However, if the list on the screen contains the item of interest then "n" prevents the scroll and gives the next menu (by use of an "ON ERROR GOTO") allows for the choice of the disc function (LOAD. MERGE. SAVE. ERASE). (It is useful to have the list on screen when typing in the name.)

Pressing "l","m"."s","E" then gives query for name. Here, if the item has been loaded, (such as for extension etc.) so that the name has already been specified then just pressing RETURN is all that is necessary.

A query to confirm is included for safety. This may seem a bit

longwinded since some of the functions(e.g.,the DIRs) may not be required. However, the menu items are skipped if any key other than "0 to 9" or "l,m,s,E" in the function menu. e.g. if one presses "d" from the main menu followed by any letter and "l"(e.g.,"ll" you get the "NAME? "query for loading from disc 1.

If you want to skip from that point "RETURN" takes you back to the main menu. To get back into text mode just press "RETURN" again.

The lines defining these features can be be used directly in OUTWRITE. (just with a change of line number).

My main Tas 2 menu has an item "PRINT".This gives the option to print in 2, 64-character columns (condensed mode). I have added this item to OUTWRITE together with a short Basic routine to perform the 2-column print function. Why on earth is the delete key not used properly to delete the character on which the cursor sits?

This is presumably because the cursor obscures the character. Please do change this! I wonder how long it will take you computer wizards to realise that required items in lists are much easier to locate if the lists are in alphabetical order, (see my article in OUTLET 51).

The Help pages need reorganising in this way. The main menu obtained on loading is weak in this way, each item should start with a key word, e.g., the first item should be "TEXT mode" and the second "DRIVE change".

The user after the first few times will need to grasp the function with least delay and certainly not to have to read a whole line before finding the word key to the function.I much prefer pop up menus (and I find most people who are using my mods agree).I found a difficulty at first with these in that one tended to find that their printing, such as by:-PRINT #0; "LOAD. SAVE. etc would cause the main text to scroll up.

This was because the control space at the bottom of the screen was over-filled.

This is easily overcome by the use of CALL 337:PRINT #0;".....

The Call clears the control space of the screen without affecting the main part.

There are quite a few other improvements which could be suggested for OUTWRITE. One example is to have the facility to use the FONTS in the print- ing. If RJW and yourselves would be interested I should be happy to co-operate in its development.

Let me add that I am full of admiration for the author of any program of the magnitude of OUTWRITE. The sheer magnitude of the task of writing and de- bugging so long a program would be quite beyond me. This alone surely makes it all the more desirable for users to put in suggestion and criticisms to help the prog reach a further stage of perfection.

Mike Haine .

Brian Cavers to Mike Haine

Thanks for all your ideas, Mike. All feedback on OUTWRITE is noted for the future upgrade. I must just make some comments in reply though...

The control keys are NOT awkward as you say but it is merely that they are not to your preference and that anything new is unfam- iliar and therefore may SEEM awkward to YOU. You speak of pressing EDIT then a key as if this is a problem. Clearly there are not enough extra keys to provide a single keypress for every function. The alternative is a SHIFTED key which differs only because you don't RELEASE between keys. Right?

You'll find all the actual disc access is in BASIC anyway so you can easily remove the DIR if required.I agree printing may be better from BASIC or at least started in BASIC so it could be modified easily, for instance, multiple copies, adding,removing a linefeed, etc.

The DELETE key IS used properly. Again, it is your concept of how it should be that conflicts. Who is the authority to say DELETE must delete the character on which the cursor is sitting? Is it written somewhere in tablets of stone? I'm happy with it. You have simply got used to just ONE method of doing it and assume it to be THE method.

I'm sorry Mike but our software is our bread and butter and I must defend it in the same mood that you attack it! If you had simply said, "I don't agree with the method used by DELETE, much preferring another method" I would have more sympathy but if you say, "Why on earth is the delete key not use properly" I have to reply in like manner!

Dear Ron and Brian

In contrast, we ourselves have strived to give good service - not because it's good for business but because we WANT to! It has made no difference: we're still struggling yet see other enterprises, ones giving a poor service, making a nice profit!

I was also thinking the other day, suppose a company sell an item at `40 and make `15 profit. Suppose the cost of replying to inquiries amounts to `2.50 each. Suppose statistics show that, on average, only 1 in 10 inquirers

follow up with a firm order. It would cost them `25 to answer those inquiries so they would lose `10 overall. Remember, you MUST include in the cost of replying not just the stationery and the stamp but the cost of paying an employee to read your letter, spend time thinking and time dictating a letter and time typing the letter. Even if you include an SAE with a form for someone to scribble on, that may be so rare that is more cost- effective for a company to give a blanket instruction to its employees - "Ignore inquiries!".

Think also of this. Suppose a company is working flat out to cope with orders. Suppose they

can't afford to employ more staff.In the mail comes 500 firm orders and 10 inquiries. The orders can be dealt with by an automatic process which is all costed and they make `15 on each one while the inquiries each take longer to deal with and, as calculated, they LOSE money on average. What do they do?

I'm not supporting them,I'm just pondering why. There has to be a reason why a company might receive a letter "This is the tenth time I've written - How much do your widgets cost?" and they throw it in the bin. Many is the time I've suffered the same "brick-wall" policy that you have so you have my fullest sympathy.

To summarise this problem...

There's just no answer!

От: Alan D. Cox, DYFED

Дорогие Ron и Brian,

Я ссылаюсь на свое предыдущее письмо о
баге «обратного листинга» и поддер-
живающий комментарий Stuart M. Burton из
Poole в выпуске OUTLET в этом месяце.

После открытого приглашения в недавнем
FORMAT я написал Andy Wright из
BETASOFT по поводу этого бага, и он
предложил объяснение, основанное на
предполагаемом использовании листингов с
отступами.

Однако я обычно не использую такие
листинги, поэтому это не решило мою
конкретную проблему.

Я нашел способ стабильно воспроизводить
этот эффект, хотя пока только с одной
конкретной программой, и отправил Andy
диск с демонстрацией. Жду его ответа.

Я указал Andy, что у Mr. Burton та же
проблема, и предположил, что как только
он найдет причину, он или я должны
написать в OUTLET еще раз.

Я не могу гарантировать, что это работает
для всех программ, но попробуйте сделать
листинг сверху, например, LIST 8000,
отклоните прокрутку, затем снизу,
например, LIST 7000, отклоните прокрутку,
а затем нажмите стрелку вверх. В моем
случае это дает цветные полосы, нало-
женные на листинг, а прикосновение к
клавиатуре вызывает полный сброс.

По второй теме: я недавно вступил в
местную группу пользователей компьютеров,
и поскольку я был единственным участником
с SAM Coupe, редактор бюллетеня попросил
меня написать статью о нем. Он хотел
статью быстро, поэтому не было времени
разбираться с переносом с компьютера на
компьютер, и ему пришлось перепечатывать
ее в свою машину (напомните мне не
вызываться редактировать бюллетень!) -
он использует PC с TOP COPY PLUS. Однако
это явно было безумием как долгосрочное
решение, поэтому мы экспериментируем с
другими методами.

Первый метод возник потому, что у
редактора осталась система Spectrum+ с
микродрайвами.

Он может перенести данные со Spectrum на
PC, используя последовательный порт
Interface 1 и команду MOVE:

```text
  10 CLOSE #4
  20 FORMAT "b";1200
  30 OPEN #4;"b"
  40 INPUT "ENTER FILE NAME";N$
  50 MOVE "M";2;N$ TO #4
  60 CLOSE #4
  70 STOP
```

На стороне PC он использует программный
пакет 'Mite', о котором я ничего не знаю,
кроме того, что он работает. Теперь,
'WORDMASTER' сохраняет документы как
CODE-файлы, так что единственное звено,
которого не хватает — это чтение SAM
CODE-файла на Spectrum (SAM, конечно,
может читать Spectrum/Disciple CODE-файл).

Однако, полагаю, неудивительно, что
обратное неверно: было бы умно со стороны
автора программного обеспечения Disciple
предусмотреть протоколы SAM!

Это не большая проблема — я полагаю, вы
делаете что-то подобное каждый день —
но для протокола: способ сделать это —
использовать команду READ AT на Disciple,
чтобы прочитать необходимое в память
Spectrum, а затем SAVE как настоящий
Spectrum CODE-файл.

SAM CODE-файлы имеют на первом секторе
девятибайтовый заголовок, за которым
следует 501 байт файла, заканчивающийся
двухбайтовым указателем на следующий
трек/сектор. Последующие треки/сектора
не имеют заголовка, но имеют указатель на
следующий трек/сектор. Удивительно, но
похоже, что в последнем секторе нет
маркера конца файла.

Таким образом, чтобы выполнить перенос,
возьмите чистый диск (т.е. переформати-
рованный или с удаленными файлами) и
сохраните SAM CODE-файл на нем. Это для
упрощения, так как вы тогда знаете, что
файл начинается на треке 4, секторе 1 и
идет по порядку. Разработать более общий
случай несложно, но в данных обстоятель-
ствах кажется мне излишним. Также
обратите внимание на длину файла.

Затем перенесите на Spectrum, вставьте
диск в привод Disciple, введите
следующую программу, затем запустите ее.
Вы получите Spectrum CODE-файл с тем же
именем, что и у SAM, с добавленной "s" в
начале и, если необходимо, обрезанный до
10 символов.

```text
 10 REM Conversion program
 20 INPUT "name of file ?";n$
 25 LET n$=n$( TO 9)
 30 INPUT "Length of file ?";L
 40 LET z=INT(L/512)+1
 50 FOR n=1 to z
 60 LOAD @1,4+INT (n/10),n-10
    *INT(n/10),40000-9+510*(n-1)
 70 NEXT n
 80 LET z$="s"+n$
 90 SAVE d1;z$CODE 40000,L
 100 STOP
```

Однако с моей точки зрения это все еще
не идеально, хотя бы потому, что я нахожу
микродрайвы раздражающими и ненадежными.
Очевидный носитель — это 3.5-дюймовые
дискеты с обеих сторон. Главная очевидная
загвоздка в том, что в то время как SAM
форматирует диск с 80 дорожками на
сторону и 10 секторами на дорожку, PC,
используя DD/DS дискеты, использует 80
дорожек на сторону, но только 9 секторов
на дорожку.

Однако, к моему удивлению, хотя сектора
должны быть разного физического размера,
SAM может читать сектора с 1 по 9 на
дорожке PC с помощью READ AT, хотя он не
любит пытаться найти десятый сектор!
Я предполагаю, что «метки» секторов на
диске должны быть электронными, а не
физическими.

Есть небольшие моменты, которые нужно
уладить, поскольку PC начинает с 2
загрузочных секторов, которые не имеют
явного аналога в SAM, а затем идут 6
секторов таблицы размещения файлов (FAT),
которая, я думаю, соответствует карте
памяти в записи каталога SAM для файла,
а затем 6 секторов чего-то под названием
Directory, что, я полагаю, похоже на
первую часть каталога SAM.

Должен признаться, что я еще не до конца
понимаю, куда PC помещает свои файлы,
так как у меня был только один пример
для экспериментов.

Если кто-либо из читателей может помочь,
я буду благодарен за информацию.

Конечно, завершающий этап эксперимента
— посмотреть, может ли PC дублировать
команду SAM READ AT. Если да, то все, что
остается на стороне SAM — это организовать
запись файлов только на сектора с 1 по 9
каждой дорожки, что не должно быть
сложно с помощью WRITE AT. Эта часть
эксперимента находится не под моим
контролем и, на мой взгляд, будет менее
интересна читателям OUTLET, поэтому я
считаю нужным сообщить вам вышеизложенное
до завершения эксперимента.

           С наилучшими пожеланиями,
           Alan D. Cox

Очевидное решение: клавиши управления текстом должны работать в текстовом режиме, а для работы с диском и печатью отдельное нажатие клавиши (в Tas2 это F9) должно вызывать меню (на Basic) для выбора номера дисковода и/или нужной функции.

Печать также лучше реализовать из BASIC.

В моей модификации для Tas2 клавиша F9 открывает всплывающее меню для выбора диска (1, 2 или выше для RAM-дисков).

Нажатие цифры тут же заменяет меню другим — с пронумерованными пунктами, позволяющими выбрать краткий DIR, полный DIR или другие варианты. Я использую DIR d "l*", который выводит список всех файлов, начинающихся на «l» (это мои файлы писем — letter files).

Возможны и другие подобные опции. Опять же, одиночное нажатие клавиши (от 1 до 9) запускает выбранный DIR. Если список длиннее экрана, то на запрос о прокрутке (scroll) можно ответить любой клавишей, кроме «n».

Однако если в списке на экране уже есть нужный пункт, то «n» останавливает прокрутку и выводит следующее меню (через «ON ERROR GOTO»), позволяющее выбрать действие с диском (LOAD, MERGE, SAVE, ERASE). Очень удобно видеть список перед глазами, когда вводишь имя файла.

Нажатие «l», «m», «s», «E» выдает запрос имени. При этом, если файл уже загружался (например, для дописки и т.д.) и имя уже было задано, достаточно просто нажать RETURN.

Для безопасности предусмотрен запрос подтверждения. Все это может показаться чересчур громоздким, поскольку некоторые функции (например, DIR) могут и не понадобиться. Однако пункты меню пропускаются, если нажать любую клавишу, кроме «0-9» или «l,m,s,E» в меню функций. Например, если в главном меню нажать «d», затем любую букву и «l» (скажем, «ll»), вы сразу получаете запрос «NAME?» для загрузки с диска 1.

Если вы хотите выйти из этого режима, RETURN вернет вас в главное меню. Чтобы вернуться в текст, просто нажмите RETURN еще раз.

Строки программы, реализующие эти возможности, можно перенести напрямую в OUTWRITE (лишь изменив нумерацию строк).

В моем главном меню Tas 2 есть пункт «PRINT». Он дает возможность печати в 2 колонки по 64 символа (в уплотненном режиме). Я добавил этот пункт в OUTWRITE вместе с короткой подпрограммой на Basic, выполняющей печать в две колонки. Страницы помощи требуют именно такой реорганизации. Главное меню, появляющееся при загрузке, в этом плане очень слабое: каждый пункт должен начинаться с ключевого слова, например, первым пунктом должен быть «TEXT mode», а вторым — «DRIVE change».

Пользователю после первых нескольких раз потребуется быстро понимать назначение функции с минимальной задержкой, и уж точно не вычитывать целую строку, прежде чем найти ключевое слово нужной функции. Я гораздо больше предпочитаю всплывающие меню (и нахожу, что большинство людей, использующих мои модификации, со мной согласны). Сначала у меня возникли трудности с ними, так как вывод на печать, вроде: `PRINT #0; "LOAD. SAVE.` и т. д. приводил к тому, что основной текст скроллился вверх.

Это происходило потому, что область управления внизу экрана переполнялась.

Это легко преодолевается с помощью:

```text
  CALL 337:PRINT #0;".....
```

Вызов CALL очищает область управления экрана, не затрагивая основную часть.

Есть еще немало других улучшений, которые можно было бы предложить для OUTWRITE. Один из примеров — возможность использовать шрифты (FONTS) при печати. Если RJW и вы будете заинтересованы, я был бы рад посодействовать в разработке.

Сама грандиозность задачи написания и отладки столь длинной программы была бы мне совершенно не по силам. Одно это определенно делает для пользователей еще более желательным вносить предложения и критику, чтобы помочь программе достичь следующей ступени совершенства.
